title: School Facilities and Procurement in Kenya (2026 Guide)
h1: School Facilities and Procurement in Kenya (2026 Guide)
description: School facilities and procurement in Kenya — planned maintenance, disciplined purchasing, asset registers, and getting value without leaks or waste.
author: SQUL Team
intro: Buildings, desks, water, power and supplies are the quiet machinery of a school — invisible when they work, crippling when they fail. Managing facilities and procurement well is how a school gets value for money and stops small leaks becoming big bills. This guide covers **school facilities and procurement in Kenya**, part of our wider guide on [how to manage a school in Kenya](/blog/how-to-manage-a-school-in-kenya).
It pairs with [school finance and budgeting](/blog/school-finance-and-budgeting-kenya), because procurement is where budgets are won or lost.

items: **Maintenance is cheaper than replacement** — planned repairs beat emergency ones.
**Leaks add up** — fuel, stationery and food wastage quietly drain the budget.
**Facilities affect learning** — desks, lighting and water are not luxuries.
**Traceability is expected** — boards and auditors want to see how money was spent.

items.title: Walk the school each term
items.text: A short inspection of buildings, water, power, and grounds surfaces most issues early.

items.title: Keep a repair list
items.text: Log every fault with a priority so it is fixed in order, not by who complains loudest.

items.title: Budget for repairs
items.text: A contingency line in the term budget prevents mid-term scrambles.

items.title: Record what was done
items.text: Repair history tells you what will fail next.

rows: Petty cash with receipts and a monthly total
Two or three quotes and one approval
Formal quotes, board approval, written contract
Annual supplier agreements, reviewed each year

blocks.title: Three quotes, one signature
blocks.text: A simple rule — multiple quotes for anything material, one named approver — prevents most procurement problems before they start.

You cannot protect what you cannot list. Keep a simple register of significant assets — laptops, equipment, furniture, vehicles — with what it is, where it lives, and who is responsible. It supports insurance, audits and accountability, and it stops items quietly disappearing.

items: **Buy to a spec** — know exactly what you need before you ask for quotes.
**Consolidate orders** — fewer, larger orders are cheaper and easier to track.
**Review suppliers annually** — loyalty should earn better terms, not complacency.
**Separate ordering from receiving** — where possible, different people, so deliveries are verified.
**Reactive maintenance** — fixing after it breaks, at a premium.
**No quotes** — buying on the first offer.
**One person ordering and receiving** — no check on deliveries.
**No repair budget** — a broken pump becomes a crisis.

faqs.question: How should a Kenyan school manage procurement?
faqs.answer: With scaled controls: petty cash with receipts for small items, multiple quotes and an approval for medium items, and formal quotes with board approval for large ones. Separate ordering from receiving where possible.

faqs.question: Why keep a school asset register?
faqs.answer: It lists significant assets with location and responsibility, supporting insurance, audits and accountability — and stops equipment quietly disappearing.

faqs.question: How do schools avoid maintenance crises?
faqs.answer: Walk the school each term, keep a prioritised repair list, and budget a contingency for repairs so fixes are planned rather than emergency.

faqs.question: How do we get better value from suppliers?
faqs.answer: Buy to a spec, consolidate orders, review suppliers annually, and seek better terms for loyalty. Fewer, larger, well-tracked orders usually cost less.
